articles.headline: OFAC Designates Entities Under Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA) and Issues General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA) on October 19, 2026. This action aims to safeguard American intellectual property from foreign threats.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC also issued associated General Licenses. These licenses are intended to provide guidance and authorization for certain transactions that would otherwise be prohibited under the PAIPA sanctions program.
Further details regarding the specific entities designated and the scope of the General Licenses are available on the Treasury Department's website.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Venezuela-related General License for Earthquake Relief Efforts
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued Venezuela-related General License 60A on October 16, 2026. This amended license specifically authorizes transactions related to earthquake relief efforts in Venezuela.

This amendment supersedes previous authorizations and aims to facilitate humanitarian aid in response to recent seismic activity in the region. The original General License 60, issued on June 25, 2026, also authorized transactions for earthquake relief efforts and was set to expire on October 23, 2026.
OFAC also released an amended Frequently Asked Question (FAQ 1263) to provide further clarity on the scope and application of the updated general license.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Iran-related Designations and Issues Amended General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on October 15, 2026, as part of ongoing efforts to counter illicit activities by the Iranian regime. These designations target individuals and entities deemed to be supporting Iran's destabilizing actions.

Concurrently, OFAC issued new and amended General Licenses and Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) related to Iran. These updates aim to clarify the scope of permissible activities and provide guidance for compliance with the evolving sanctions regime.

The U.S. Treasury has been actively conducting 'Operation Economic Outcast' to financially isolate Iran, expanding secondary sanctions risk under Executive Order 13902 for individuals and entities supporting various Iranian economic sectors.

articles.headline: OFAC Removes Venezuela-related Designation for National Assembly President Jorge Rodriguez
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced the removal of a Venezuela-related designation on October 14, 2026. This action specifically delisted Jorge Rodriguez, the president of Venezuela's National Assembly.
The delisting of Rodriguez comes amid a broader push by the U.S. for bilateral diplomacy and energy pacts with Venezuela.
Rodriguez, who has served as head of Venezuela's legislature since 2021, was previously sanctioned under the Trump administration due to his ministerial roles.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations on October 13, 2026. These designations target individuals and entities involved in illicit drug trafficking and terrorist financing activities globally.
These actions are part of ongoing efforts by the U.S. government to disrupt and dismantle international criminal networks that pose a threat to national security and global stability.
The designations aim to sever financial lifelines and restrict the ability of these illicit actors to operate within the international financial system.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces Settlement with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics and International Criminal Court Designation
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a settlement agreement with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics on October 9, 2026. This settlement addresses apparent violations of OFAC administered sanctions programs.

In a separate action on the same date, OFAC also announced a designation related to the International Criminal Court (ICC) and issued associated General Licenses. This designation is part of broader U.S. policy regarding the ICC.
Additionally, OFAC announced a Burma-related designation removal, indicating a recalibration of sanctions pertaining to Myanmar.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Russia-related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued a new Russia-related General License on October 9, 2026. This license authorizes certain transactions that would otherwise be prohibited under existing sanctions against Russia.
The issuance of new general licenses often indicates a refinement of sanctions policy, aiming to facilitate specific types of activities while maintaining pressure on the sanctioned regime.
Details of the authorized transactions and any associated conditions are available in the official publication of the General License.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Iran-related Designations and Amends Russia-related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on October 8, 2026. These actions are part of the ongoing 'Operation Economic Outcast' to target Iran's illicit financial activities and shadow fleet network.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC also issued a new Iran-related General License, providing specific authorizations for certain transactions. This aims to balance sanctions pressure with humanitarian or other policy considerations.

Furthermore, OFAC issued an amended Russia-related General License, indicating adjustments to existing sanctions against Russia. This amendment could reflect evolving geopolitical considerations or a need to clarify previous guidance.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces Designations Removals, Updates, and Iran-related Alert
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced several designations removals and updates on October 5, 2026. These actions reflect ongoing reviews of sanctions lists and adjustments based on new information or policy considerations.

Additionally, OFAC published an Iran-related Alert, warning foreign financial institutions about the risks of doing business with Iran's financial sector. The alert emphasizes that institutions continuing to transact with sanctioned Iranian financial institutions may face sanctions under 'Operation Economic Outcast.'
OFAC also published an amended Iran-related Frequently Asked Question, providing further guidance on compliance with Iran sanctions.

articles.headline: EU Adopts 22nd Sanctions Package Against Russia, Targeting Military-Industrial Complex
body: The European Union adopted its 22nd package of sanctions against Russia on October 12, 2026, marking one of the most significant sanctions developments since 2022.

This package adds 1,569 individuals and entities to the EU sanctions lists, comprising 826 Russian companies and 743 individuals, bringing the total number of designations under the Ukraine-related sanctions regime to almost 4,600.

The measures primarily target Russia's military-industrial complex, including companies involved in the production and supply of components used in missiles, drones, military aircraft, and related defense technologies, in response to Russia's continuing aggression against Ukraine.

articles.headline: EU Sanctions Three Individuals and Four Entities Over DPRK Nuclear and Missile Programs, Russia Ties
body: The Council of the European Union adopted additional restrictive measures against three individuals and four entities on October 12, 2026, under its autonomous sanctions list on the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK).

These designations target those responsible for supporting, promoting, or facilitating activities that contribute to the DPRK's nuclear weapons, ballistic missile, or other weapons of mass destruction programs, as well as for violating and evading United Nations sanctions.

The new listings specifically address activities linked to the growing military and economic cooperation between the DPRK and Russia, including the deployment of DPRK workers in Russia, commercial and industrial cooperation, and the 'arms-for-oil' trade, all in violation of UN Security Council prohibitions.
articles.source: Council of the EU / European Union

articles.headline: OFAC Expands Cuba Sanctions and Tightens Financial and Travel Restrictions
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has expanded its Cuba sanctions program and tightened financial and travel restrictions, effective September 30, 2026.
Under the amended regulations, persons subject to U.S. jurisdiction are no longer generally authorized to attend or organize professional meetings or conferences in Cuba.

OFAC has adopted a limited wind-down authorization through October 30, 2026, for certain persons already in Cuba under the former authorization, and educational travel to Cuba must now be under the auspices of a U.S.-jurisdiction organization, with most travelers requiring accompaniment by a sponsoring organization representative.

articles.headline: President Trump Waives New Russia Sanctions Under Graham Act Citing National Interests
body: President Donald Trump signed an executive order on October 16, 2026, waiving newly enacted sanctions against Russia under the legislation known as the Graham Act, citing U.S. national interests.

The order suspends several planned Russia-related sanctions, including tariffs on Russian imports and penalties targeting countries purchasing Russian oil and gas, which were due to take effect two days later.
The Graham Act, signed into law on September 18, 2026, had called for significant increases in tariffs on Russian goods and on goods from countries knowingly purchasing Russian oil or gas.

This settlement resolves apparent violations of various sanctions programs administered by OFAC, including those related to Iran, Russia, narcotics, and global terrorism.

The enforcement action was part of a coordinated effort by the U.S. Treasury Department, which also included significant penalties from FinCEN and the OCC against Bank of America for AML and BSA deficiencies.

articles.headline: OCC Imposes Record $750 Million Penalty on Bank of America for BSA/AML Deficiencies
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) announced a $750 million civil money penalty against Bank of America, N.A. on October 13, 2026, for widespread violations of the Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) and its implementing regulations.
This penalty, the largest in OCC history, stems from the bank's deficient and ineffective BSA/AML compliance program, which failed to properly monitor trillions of dollars in transactions.

Despite a December 2024 cease-and-desist order requiring the bank to address its longstanding BSA deficiencies, the OCC found that Bank of America's compliance program continued to exhibit widespread breakdowns in internal controls, posing a threat to U.S. national and economic security.
articles.source: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC)

articles.headline: OCC Assesses $350 Million Civil Money Penalty Against American Express

articles.headline: FinCEN Assesses $1.2 Billion Penalty Against Bank of America for BSA Violations
body: The Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) announced a $1.2 billion penalty against Bank of America, N.A. on October 13, 2026, for willful violations of the Bank Secrecy Act (BSA).
The penalty addresses the bank's failure to mitigate and report priority national security risks, including Chinese money laundering networks and illicit finance along the southwest border.

Bank of America admitted to willfully violating the BSA by failing to implement and maintain an adequate AML program, conduct due diligence for correspondent accounts for foreign financial institutions, and file Suspicious Activity Reports in a timely manner.
articles.source: U.S. Department of the Treasury FinCEN

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.

articles.headline: Enhanced Favorable Treatment for the United Arab Emirates Under the Export Administration Regulations
body: In this final rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to provide enhanced favorable treatment for the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Specifically, BIS is removing the UAE from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 and adding the UAE to Country Group A:5. More license exceptions will now be available, including Strategic Trade Authorization (STA) for the UAE Government and approved commercial entities in the UAE. STA will authorize the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) of military items; certain commercial satellites and spacecraft; and dual-use items useful in, inter alia, oil and gas production, desalination, and civil nuclear power generation. The UAE Government and approved commercial entities will also have license-free access to advanced computing items, consistent with the May 2025 U.S.-UAE Artificial Intelligence Cooperation framework, without compromising U.S. digital infrastructure buildout.
